Front: Why should constructors validate invariants?
Back: They prevent invalid objects from existing.
Extra: If invalid state is allowed at construction time, every later method must defend against it. Constructor validation centralizes that rule. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/constructors.html

Front: Why can adding one parameterized constructor break existing code?
Back: The compiler stops generating the no-argument default constructor.
Extra: When you declare a constructor like `User(String name)`, the compiler does not generate the implicit no-arg constructor `User()`. Any existing calls to `new User()` will produce a compile-time error: constructor User in class User cannot be applied to given types.

Front: Why is `this.name = name` common in constructors?
Back: It distinguishes the field from the parameter with the same name.
Extra: Without `this`, `name = name` would assign the parameter to itself and leave the field unchanged. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/thiskey.html

Front: Why does assigning `Student b = a;` not copy the object?
Back: It copies only the reference value.
Extra: Both variables point to the same heap object, so mutating through one reference is visible through the other. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/objectcreation.html

Front: Why is Java still pass-by-value with objects?
Back: The copied value is the reference value.
Extra: The callee can mutate the object through the copied reference, but reassigning the parameter does not reassign the caller variable. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/arguments.html

Front: Why are getters and setters not automatically good encapsulation?
Back: They can expose raw storage rather than meaningful behavior.
Extra: A setter that accepts any value can break invariants. Good encapsulation exposes operations that keep the object valid. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why return a defensive copy from a getter for a mutable list?
Back: To prevent callers from mutating internal state directly.
Extra: Returning the original list lets callers call `clear`, `add`, or `remove` without validation. A copy protects the field. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: Why should fields be private by default?
Back: Because fields are implementation details.
Extra: Private fields let you change representation later without breaking caller code. Public fields freeze your internal design into the API. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: Why should inheritance represent IS-A?
Back: Because callers expect the subclass to behave as a valid superclass.
Extra: This aligns with the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP). For example, if a `Penguin` subclass inherits from `Bird` but throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when `fly()` is called, it violates IS-A and breaks code that polymorphically calls `fly()` on all `Bird` instances.

Front: Why is composition often safer for code reuse than inheritance?
Back: It reuses behavior without forcing an is-a hierarchy.
Extra: Inheritance exposes a subclass to details of its parent class, creating a tight coupling (fragile base class problem). With composition, you reference an instance: `class Car { private Engine e; }`, which lets you swap behaviors or change the `Engine` class without modifying the `Car` class's public contract.

Front: Why does Java avoid multiple class inheritance?
Back: To avoid ambiguous inherited state and method implementations.
Extra: If two parent classes define conflicting behavior, a child extending both would need ambiguous resolution rules. Java uses interfaces for multiple contracts. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/subclasses.html

Front: Why must `super(...)` or `this(...)` be first in a constructor?
Back: Superclass or peer constructor initialization must happen before the rest of the constructor body.
Extra: The object must be initialized from the top of the hierarchy downward before child-specific initialization can safely run. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/constructors.html

Front: Why can an overriding method not be more restrictive?
Back: It would break substitutability through the superclass type.
Extra: If callers can invoke a public parent method, a child object must still support that call when used polymorphically. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/override.html

Front: Why are static methods not runtime polymorphic?
Back: Static methods belong to the class and are resolved by reference type.
Extra: They do not dispatch through the actual heap object. This is why hiding differs from overriding. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/override.html

Front: Why are fields not polymorphic?
Back: Field access is resolved by compile-time reference type.
Extra: Only overridden instance methods use dynamic dispatch. A hidden child field does not replace the parent field polymorphically. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/override.html

Front: Why can return type alone not overload a method?
Back: The caller might ignore the return value, making the call ambiguous.
Extra: If we have `int calculate()` and `double calculate()`, and call `calculate();` without assigning the result, the compiler cannot know which method to run. Thus, method signatures in Java are defined only by the method name and the number, type, and order of its parameters.

Front: Why is dynamic dispatch useful?
Back: It lets code depend on a common type while behavior comes from the actual object.
Extra: Dynamic dispatch resolves overridden instance methods at runtime based on the actual heap object. For example, if `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` is called, the JVM dispatches `Dog.speak()` via the class's virtual method table (vtable), allowing polymorphically writing logic like `a.speak()` for any `Animal` subclass.

Front: Why can frequent downcasting be a design smell?
Back: It means the abstraction may not expose the behavior callers actually need.
Extra: If callers constantly ask “what concrete type is this?”, polymorphism is not carrying enough of the design. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/polymorphism.html

Front: Why use `instanceof` before downcasting?
Back: To avoid `ClassCastException`.
Extra: Downcasting is explicit and risky: `Dog d = (Dog) animal;` throws `ClassCastException` at runtime if the object is actually a `Cat`. In Java 16+, pattern matching simplifies this check and cast to a single line: `if (animal instanceof Dog d) { d.bark(); }`.

Front: Why can abstract classes hold state while interfaces cannot hold instance state?
Back: An abstract class participates in a class hierarchy; an interface defines a contract.
Extra: An abstract class can declare instance fields (e.g. `private int score;`) and constructors to initialize them when a subclass object is instantiated. Interfaces cannot declare instance fields; any field declared inside an interface is implicitly `public static final` (a constant).

Front: Why is using an interface as a type powerful?
Back: It lets callers depend on a contract rather than a concrete implementation.
Extra: Depending on an interface like `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();` allows you to switch the implementation to `LinkedList` or an unmodifiable list later without changing the rest of the codebase. It also simplifies testing by allowing you to easily inject mock implementations of the interface.

Front: Why were default methods added to interfaces?
Back: To evolve interfaces without breaking every existing implementer.
Extra: A new abstract method would force all implementing classes to change. A default method can provide fallback behavior. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/defaultmethods.html

Front: What happens if two interfaces provide the same default method?
Back: The implementing class must resolve the conflict.
Extra: If both interfaces `A` and `B` define a default `void print()` method, implementing both leads to a compile-time error due to method signature conflict. The class must override `print()` and can optionally delegate to one of them using the syntax: `A.super.print();`.

Front: What is the practical difference between identity and capability?
Back: Abstract classes usually model identity; interfaces usually model capability.
Extra: `Account` as an abstract class can share balance state. `Payable` as an interface can be implemented by unrelated classes. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/abstract.html

Front: Why is a class called a blueprint rather than the object itself?
Back: The class describes what objects can have and do; objects are the runtime instances created from that description.
Extra: Changing a field on one object does not change every object of that class. The class is the design; each object has its own identity and instance state. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: Why are identity, state, and behavior separated when describing objects?
Back: They answer different questions about the same object.
Extra: Identity asks "which object is this?", state asks "what values does it hold?", and behavior asks "what can it do?". This separation prevents confusion between two equal-looking objects and one shared object referenced twice. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/objectcreation.html

Front: Why are fields not the same thing as the object itself?
Back: Fields are only the stored data inside an object.
Extra: The object also has identity and behavior. If a field changes, the object can still be the same object. If two objects have equal field values, they can still be distinct objects. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: Why should behavior usually be modeled as methods instead of public fields?
Back: Methods let the object control how its state changes.
Extra: Public fields let callers bypass validation and domain rules. Methods can name intent, enforce invariants, and keep representation private. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why is constructor work more than assigning fields?
Back: A constructor establishes the first valid state of an object.
Extra: It should validate required values, normalize inputs when appropriate, and make sure the object can be safely used immediately after `new`. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/constructors.html

Front: How can accidentally writing a return type on a constructor change the program?
Back: It becomes a method, not a constructor.
Extra: `void User()` looks constructor-like but is a normal method named `User`. The real constructor is missing, so initialization may not happen when the object is created. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/constructors.html

Front: Why does declaring any constructor remove the implicit no-argument constructor?
Back: The compiler assumes you are taking control of construction.
Extra: If you declare `User(String name)`, Java will not also invent `User()`. Add `User()` explicitly if callers or frameworks need it. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/constructors.html

Front: Why is constructor overloading useful but easy to misuse?
Back: It supports different creation paths, but those paths must keep the same invariants.
Extra: Good overloaded constructors delegate to one canonical constructor with `this(...)`. Bad overloaded constructors duplicate validation and slowly drift apart. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/thiskey.html

Front: Why does `this` help avoid shadowing bugs?
Back: It makes field access explicit when a parameter has the same name.
Extra: In `this.name = name`, the left side is the object's field and the right side is the parameter. Without `this`, `name = name` can silently assign the parameter to itself. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/thiskey.html

Front: Why must constructor chaining with `this(...)` be first?
Back: Another constructor must initialize the object before the current constructor continues.
Extra: If ordinary statements ran first, Java would allow partially initialized setup before the chosen constructor path. The first-statement rule keeps construction order clear. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/thiskey.html

Front: Why is an object reference not the object itself?
Back: The reference is a value used to access an object.
Extra: Multiple variables can hold copies of the same reference value and reach the same object. This is why aliasing matters when objects are mutable. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/objectcreation.html

Front: Why does Java pass-by-value still allow object mutation inside a method?
Back: The method receives a copied reference value that still points to the same object.
Extra: Mutating through the copied reference changes the shared object. Reassigning the parameter only changes the local copy of the reference. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/arguments.html

Front: When is an anonymous object acceptable?
Back: When the object is used immediately and does not need to be referenced again.
Extra: For example, passing `new Task()` directly to a method can be clean. If the object needs reuse, inspection, or later mutation, store the reference in a variable. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/objectcreation.html

Front: Why are invariants central to OOP design?
Back: They define what it means for an object to be valid.
Extra: Without invariants, methods must handle impossible or nonsensical states everywhere. Encapsulation and constructors work together to make invalid states hard to create. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why can `==` and `.equals()` answer different object questions?
Back: `==` checks reference identity; `.equals()` can check logical equality.
Extra: Two different `String` objects may be logically equal even if they are not the same object. For custom classes, `.equals()` should match the equality rule your domain needs. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/objectcreation.html

Front: Why is encapsulation more than making fields private?
Back: Private fields are only the access-control part.
Extra: True encapsulation designs a public API that preserves valid state, hides representation choices, and expresses behavior in domain terms. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why does data hiding make code easier to change later?
Back: Callers depend on behavior instead of storage details.
Extra: If `age` changes from a stored field to a computed value, callers using `getAge()` may not need to change. Public fields make representation changes expensive. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: Why is `private` not only about security?
Back: It is mostly about protecting object consistency and API design.
Extra: `private` does not stop all possible access in every advanced runtime scenario, but it prevents ordinary code from coupling to internal representation. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: When can a getter still break encapsulation?
Back: When it returns a mutable internal object directly.
Extra: A getter returning the actual internal `List` lets callers mutate the object without validation. Return an unmodifiable view or defensive copy when needed. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: When is a setter a bad design choice?
Back: When it allows arbitrary state changes without domain meaning or validation.
Extra: `setBalance(-1000)` is weaker than behavior such as `withdraw(amount)` with validation. Behavior methods reveal intent and keep invariants close to the data. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why does defensive copying matter specifically for mutable reference fields?
Back: The reference points to an object that someone else may modify.
Extra: If a constructor stores a caller's mutable list directly, the caller can change the object's internal state after construction. Copy on input and output when ownership matters. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/javaOO/index.html

Front: How can read-only APIs still expose useful behavior?
Back: They can provide queries and operations that do not mutate state.
Extra: A class can expose `size()`, `contains(x)`, or `total()` without exposing setters. Read-only does not mean useless; it means mutation is controlled. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why are behavior methods often better names for business rules?
Back: They describe intent rather than storage mutation.
Extra: `approve()`, `deposit(amount)`, or `markCompleted()` tells readers what rule is being applied. Raw setters only say a field changed. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: How does encapsulation reduce coupling between classes?
Back: It narrows what callers are allowed to know.
Extra: Callers use stable public methods while the class is free to reorganize fields, helper methods, validation, and caching internally. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/

Front: Why is inheritance powerful but risky?
Back: It reuses and specializes behavior, but tightly couples subclass behavior to superclass design.
Extra: A superclass change can affect all subclasses. Use inheritance when the parent was designed to be extended and the subclass is truly substitutable. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/subclasses.html

Front: What does a stable IS-A relationship mean in practice?
Back: A subclass should be safely usable anywhere the superclass is expected.
Extra: If `Square` cannot honor all expectations of `Rectangle`, then the IS-A claim is mathematically tempting but behaviorally dangerous. Substitutability matters more than naming. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/subclasses.html

Front: Why does single class inheritance simplify Java object layout and behavior?
Back: There is only one direct superclass chain.
Extra: This avoids many conflicts around inherited fields, constructors, and concrete implementations. Java uses interfaces to express multiple contracts without multiple inherited object state. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/subclasses.html

Front: Why is knowing the superclass important when reading code?
Back: The superclass may define inherited methods, fields, constructor requirements, and behavioral promises.
Extra: A subclass file may not show everything the object can do. You often need to inspect the parent to understand available behavior and initialization rules. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/subclasses.html

Front: Why should subclasses avoid surprising their superclass callers?
Back: Polymorphic code treats the subclass as the superclass.
Extra: If overridden behavior violates the parent contract, existing code that worked with the parent may fail with the child. This is a core substitutability problem. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/override.html

Front: Why does `super` not mean "any ancestor class"?
Back: `super` targets the immediate superclass relationship from the current class.
Extra: It is used to call the parent constructor, parent implementation, or hidden parent member. For deeper ancestors, access must still go through the inheritance chain rules. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/subclasses.html
